articles.title: Setting a new standard for responsible AI infrastructure
articles.description: OpenAI introduces its National Community Compact and Compute Campus Policy Blueprint to protect local resources, create jobs, and guide responsible AI infrastructure development.
articles.full_text:
Title: Setting a new standard for responsible AI infrastructure

URL Source: https://openai.com/index/setting-new-standard-responsible-ai-infrastructure

Final URL: https://openai.com/index/setting-new-standard-responsible-ai-infrastructure/

Markdown Content:
The promise of AI is that it gives people more power to shape their own futures. It can help someone learn a new skill, build a business, or solve a problem that was previously out of reach. Building more computing infrastructure capacity in the United States can help lower the cost of delivering AI, put these tools in more people’s hands, and ensure America stays at the forefront of the technology.

The communities that host this infrastructure should have a clear say in shaping their futures, too. Residents should be able to influence how a campus is developed, hold developers accountable for covering the cost of powering it, and share in the jobs and business opportunities it creates. How we build these campuses is one of the first tests of whether the benefits of AI will be broadly shared.

Today we’re publishing our [National Community Compact⁠(opens in a new window)](https://cdn.openai.com/pdf/community-compact.pdf) and a [Compute Campus Policy Blueprint⁠(opens in a new window)](https://cdn.openai.com/pdf/compute-campus-policy-blueprint.pdf). The compact sets out what communities can expect from OpenAI at future campuses that we own and operate. The blueprint proposes policies to help ensure that compute campus development gives communities a meaningful voice, protects families from new costs, and broadly shares the economic gains of AI.

This builds on work we began in January, when we announced our [Stargate Community commitments](https://openai.com/index/stargate-community/) to pay our own way on energy and develop plans shaped by local priorities. We followed with specific commitments in [Georgia](https://openai.com/index/building-ai-infrastructure-with-the-effingham-county-community/) and[Ohio](https://openai.com/index/openai-joins-ports-pike-project/), covering energy costs, water use, local investment and accountability. Throughout that work, we’ve listened to residents, local leaders, schools and businesses about what matters to their communities. Today’s announcement is the next step in that ongoing effort.

## Our commitments to the communities where we build

Every future compute campus OpenAI owns and operates will have its own local compact. We’ll engage residents early enough to ensure their input shapes project plans, give them a local point of contact throughout the life of the campus, and report publicly each year on how we’re doing. Each compact will reflect local priorities and include a common set of commitments:

*   **Pay our own way on energy and infrastructure.** We’ll pay the full cost of the electricity we use and the infrastructure needed to serve us. Before major spending begins, we’ll provide financial assurances so other customers are protected if a project is delayed, reduced, or canceled.

*   **Protect local resources and report on our impact.**We’ll develop a water plan for each campus, prioritize closed-loop or low-water cooling, and publish site-level water and electricity use. We’ll publish construction plans and independent noise studies before operations begin and annually afterward. And we will not use non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) with public officials, allowing only narrow protections covering legitimate security information, trade secrets, or proprietary or competitively sensitive information.

*   **Create opportunities for local workers and businesses.**We’ll publish the jobs we expect to create, work with unions and training providers to help residents prepare for them, and report annually on hiring and apprenticeships. We’ll also make sustained investments in priorities residents help select.

Those priorities will differ from place to place. In Effingham County, Georgia, residents helped shape a $4.8 million grant to provide free school meals for all 14,000 students in the county. In Pike County, Ohio, families identified childcare as a priority, leading to a joint $6 million commitment from OpenAI and SB Energy.

## A policy blueprint for responsible development

Families should be able to count on basic protections whoever builds a campus in their community. Voluntary commitments from companies are an important starting point, but our blueprint goes further—asking federal, state, and local policymakers to establish clear rules for how the industry builds. New policy is required to establish trust and confidence between communities, elected officials and companies. Lawmakers should establish rules to advance responsible investment, protect residents, and ensure that the benefits of AI infrastructure are broadly shared.

That starts with who pays for power. State utility commissions should require large electricity customers to cover the costs they add to the grid and protect other customers if a project falls through. Utilities should also make it easier for campuses to connect if they can safely cut demand when power is scarce. At our planned Effingham County campus, for example, our agreement with Georgia Power allows the utility to reduce the power it delivers to us by up to 1,000 megawatts during periods of high demand. Congress can help meet growing demand by speeding up transmission upgrades and restoring and expanding tax incentives for clean electricity.

Communities also need a way to hold developers accountable. The blueprint calls for public reporting on water, energy, noise, and hiring, and for narrow limits on when developers can require public officials to sign NDAs. When states or local governments offer tax incentives, the terms should be public, with measurable commitments and a way to recover benefits if a developer falls short.

Finally, the blueprint proposes practical ways to keep more of the work local to ensure compute campuses support local workers and local businesses. Developers can share purchasing plans early enough for local suppliers to compete for contracts. Employers, building trades unions, and community colleges can use hiring forecasts to train residents for jobs they know will be available, from electrical work during construction to maintaining power and cooling systems for years afterward.

## Building from the community up

The investments that help America compete globally can also help communities prosper locally. That starts with giving residents a say while plans can still change and a way to hold developers accountable for delivering on their commitments. That’s what we’re committing to at the campuses we own and operate, and what we believe people should be able to count on wherever AI infrastructure is built across the country.

articles.title: Flipsnack grows product signups with conversion optimization
articles.description: Flipsnack focused its ChatGPT Ads campaigns on getting people to try its product, growing registrations while lowering the cost per signup.
articles.full_text:
Title: Flipsnack grows product signups with conversion optimization

URL Source: https://openai.com/ads/customers/flipsnack

Final URL: https://openai.com/ads/customers/flipsnack/

Markdown Content:
## Results at a glance

~75%

lower cost per registration in five US conversion-focused campaigns than in their earlier click-focused versions, which used fixed bids.¹

~310%

more registrations in those same five conversion-focused campaigns compared with their earlier click-focused versions.¹

## Connecting a versatile product to a specific need

[Flipsnack⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.flipsnack.com/) helps teams turn static documents into interactive digital experiences. Its customers use the platform to create product catalogs, sales presentations, brochures, internal communications, and training materials.

For Flipsnack, that range of applications creates a marketing challenge: helping people recognize how the product fits the work they need to do. As the company increased its focus on business customers, it wanted to reach people with needs that its product category alone might not clearly describe.

Flipsnack had relied heavily on search advertising. Its ChatGPT Ads test became an opportunity to learn which customer needs could translate into product signups.

## Measuring the action that brings people into the product

Because Flipsnack is a visual product, prospective customers often want to experience it before speaking with sales. Its campaign landing pages directed people into a signup flow, making completed registration the first meaningful step the team could measure and optimize for.

To help business customers see where the product could fit their work, Flipsnack expanded beyond its original, broader Flipbook campaign. Separate campaigns for Magazine, Catalog, and Brochure addressed specific document needs, while campaigns for Sales Enablement, Employee Benefits, Real Estate, and Hospitality connected the product to business applications and industries.

> “A sales team and an internal communications team can use the same product for very different jobs. We want our campaigns to help each see where Flipsnack fits.”

—Paul Romancsak, Paid Advertising Manager at Flipsnack

Flipsnack’s initial click-focused campaigns brought in traffic and signups. After seeing better delivery and registration efficiency in conversion-focused campaigns, the team rebuilt existing campaigns with a conversions objective and bidding set to maximize conversions.

![Image 1: Flipsnack ad showing an internal newsletter, PDF and PowerPoint icons, and the text: Make PDFs interactive. Add videos and clickable links. Track reader engagement.](https://openai.com/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fcdn.openai.com%2Fmdx-assets%2F67bd281e-a14e-4cb9-94f8-96bd17b694f6%2Fflipsnack-chatgpt-ad-3x.7f4a2348.png&w=3840&q=90)

A Flipsnack ad in ChatGPT.

## Improving registration efficiency

Flipsnack created conversion-focused versions of five existing US campaigns that had used a clicks objective with fixed bids.

Early results following the shift to conversion-focused campaigns were encouraging. Across five campaigns, registrations increased approximately 310% while cost per registration fell approximately 75%, with daily budget settings unchanged.[1](https://openai.com/ads/customers/flipsnack/#user-content-fn-1)

> “What stood out was that we were getting more registrations at a lower cost per signup. That gave us the confidence to make conversion optimization the focus of our campaigns.”

—Paul Romancsak, Paid Advertising Manager at Flipsnack

## Building on registration results

These results give Flipsnack a promising foundation for continued growth with ChatGPT Ads. Building on its conversion-focused campaigns, the team aims to bring more prospective customers into the product and help them discover how Flipsnack can support their business.

## Advertise in ChatGPT

Reach people as they explore options, compare choices, and make decisions in ChatGPT, with relevant ads that fit naturally into the experience.

[Start now (opens in a new window)](https://ads.openai.com/)

## Footnotes

1.   1
Results are based on Flipsnack’s ChatGPT Ads Manager data for five US campaign pairs, August 25–31 versus September 2–8, 2026, checked September 11. Attribution uses 30-day clicks, excluding views. Daily budget limits were unchanged; spend rose approximately 1.3%. Objectives and bidding changed together.[](https://openai.com/ads/customers/flipsnack/#user-content-fnref-1)

articles.title: Franklin Templeton uses OpenAI to support investment research
articles.description: Starting with equity research, Franklin Templeton is developing AI workflows to help portfolio managers compare research views and examine investment risks.
articles.full_text:
Title: Franklin Templeton uses OpenAI to support investment research

URL Source: https://openai.com/index/franklin-templeton

Final URL: https://openai.com/index/franklin-templeton/

Markdown Content:
Franklin Templeton wants AI to help portfolio managers examine different research views and the risks behind an investment idea. Codex is one of several tools our investment teams are using to develop workflows for investment research.

> “The biggest unlock from using OpenAI’s tools is the ability to merge continuous intelligence with human judgment. It has really transitioned because, beforehand, AI was automating our human-led process. Now AI is actually automating the ability to surface intelligent insights, and that intelligence layer plus human judgment is just a fantastic unlock.”

—Katrina Dudley, Senior Vice President, Public Market Investments, Franklin Templeton

Franklin Templeton on using OpenAI for investment research

## Creating connected, continuous intelligence

When Franklin Templeton first tried using AI, the team put data in a database and connected the models to it. But it didn’t produce the answers the teams needed because the models didn’t understand how the data fit together. When the team added agents and a semantic layer, a structured model of what the firm’s data means and how it’s connected, the results changed. The team is using Codex and other tools to develop this connected intelligence layer. "We've been able to build what we think of as a connected intelligence layer," Dudley says. "We're bringing the data into the tools, and we're surfacing insights that make a difference."

Research, risk, compliance, and trading offer different perspectives on an investment. Franklin Templeton’s ambition is to bring those inputs together for portfolio managers. “We're able to bring that all in and then use that to surface insights to the people who are making decisions, which are our portfolio managers,” Dudley says.

Dudley describes the earlier equity-research workflow as human-led and sequential: an analyst performs first-pass stock analysis, reviews earnings calls, and studies competitors in each business line. The goal is to surface useful information as analysts prepare new ideas to be pitched to portfolio managers or provide updates on existing positions in the portfolio. As she puts it, “It's just continuous intelligence combined with that human judgment.”

In the workflow Franklin Templeton envisions, its investment teams will have access to a governed, reusable intelligence foundation that brings together trusted connectors, portfolio and workflow context, and agentic capabilities that surface actionable insights for its analysts and portfolio managers.

## Creating workflows specific to each role

Franklin Templeton has used Codex in hackathons, bringing experts alongside investment practitioners as they develop their own tools. Its Investment AI champions are working to turn experiments into production-ready workflows, with security review, expert support, and data controls as part of that process.

Dudley says, “We have moved from augmenting our research process to reimagining the investment research workflow.”

## Building AI around how investing works

Some of what makes AI helpful in other settings doesn't work in asset management. Many tools learn a user's preferences and show them more of the same, so if someone favors one research provider, the tool surfaces more of that provider's reports. For an investment team, that narrowing potentially brings a biased perspective into the investment process. Franklin Templeton wants the opposite. "We want to make sure that they're accessing that diversity of research and diversity of opinion," Dudley says.

Franklin Templeton wants its AI systems to emphasize investment risks. “We need AI to understand that a great investment idea is one that is well reasoned, but it also has analyzed the risks and makes our portfolio managers aware of the risk,” Dudley says. “If you’re looking at a research note, focusing on the fact someone has identified the investment risks is not a bad thing from our perspective. It makes for a more informed investment decision.”

Franklin Templeton's experience points to some investment management best practices:

*   “Our message from leadership is consistent: we encourage innovation and experimentation with AI within clearly defined risk guardrails. Not every initiative will succeed, but each should generate insights that strengthen our capabilities, inform future decisions, and drive continuous improvement,” Dudley says.

*   Get new tools into people's hands: Dudley says Franklin Templeton has brought practical labs to teams quickly after new technology launches, so they can test how it fits their work.

*   Help teams learn the tools: Dudley says, "The goal is getting them to actually understand the power of the technology."

*   Build with appropriate controls: Security review, expert support, and data agreements are part of Franklin Templeton’s path from experimentation toward production-grade tools.

> “With OpenAI, our teams feel like they’re at the forefront of technology.”

—Katrina Dudley, Senior Vice President, Public Market Investments, Franklin Templeton

Dudley’s longer-term goal is to make that connected intelligence accessible across investment teams, from analysts to the leaders of each investment group.

She wants analysts to spend more time in the field, speaking with many different experts and professionals, including executives at private companies, and bringing what they learn back to their investment teams. For Dudley, that human perspective remains essential as the tools develop.

articles.title: OpenAI to acquire Pierre Computer Company, Inc.
articles.description: OpenAI will acquire Pierre Computer Company, expanding Codex’s tools for building, understanding, and reviewing code.
articles.full_text:
Title: OpenAI to acquire Pierre Computer Company, Inc.

URL Source: https://openai.com/index/openai-to-acquire-pierre

Final URL: https://openai.com/index/openai-to-acquire-pierre/

Markdown Content:
Today we're announcing that OpenAI will acquire [Pierre Computer Company, Inc⁠(opens in a new window)](https://pierre.computer/). (“Pierre”), the company behind [Code Storage⁠(opens in a new window)](https://code.storage/) and a family of standout open-source developer tools. If you’ve browsed files or reviewed a change in the Codex app, you’ve already used Pierre’s Trees and Diffs libraries. We’re excited to work with the Pierre team to build on the Git workflows that developers already rely on and adapt them to how teams work with coding agents.

We’ve seen in our own engineering work how the systems around Git need to evolve as more of that work happens in parallel. Earlier this week, we shared how we’re [scaling Git at OpenAI](https://openai.com/index/scaling-git-at-openai/) with Pando, our in-house source control backend for engineers and agents. With the Pierre team, we wish to set the standard for modern software development: from the first branch an agent creates to that magic moment when code is deployed to the world. We want to make Codex the place where developers and agents take on their most ambitious projects.

## Craftsmanship meets scale for the agentic era

We’ve long appreciated the care Pierre brings to another part of working with Git: how developers review code. You can see that care in the libraries we use in Codex today. Trees lets developers quickly navigate a project’s files, and Diffs makes it easy to see what changed. Both of these tools make it easy to review and navigate large volumes of code with uncompromising performance.

That same attention to detail runs through Pierre’s other work. Diffs’ _Edit_ mode lets a reviewer fix a line of code right where they spot the problem. Pierre recently released _Highlights_, an extremely fast syntax highlighter that updates as a developer types or an agent streams code. The same small team that put an editor inside a diff also designed the API for Code Storage, a service that lets apps store code and track its history using Git.

## Bringing the work together in Codex

Pierre has built tools that developers love, and together, we will ship new products and platforms that benefit all. Once the acquisition closes, our ambition is to advance the future of source control across the industry. We want Codex to connect the code a company ships with the decisions its people make, at the scale the future demands.

Pierre’s open-source projects will remain open-source, and we’ll continue to contribute to them. Customers can continue using Code Storage after the acquisition closes while we work to bring its features and functionality into Codex.

_The closing of the acquisition is subject to customary closing conditions, including receipt of regulatory approvals. Until closing, OpenAI and Pierre will remain separate and independent companies._

articles.title: A thousand fewer paths to root
articles.description: OpenAI built an autonomous pipeline that found, validated, and generated patches for 948 local privilege-escalation vulnerabilities in the Linux kernel.
articles.full_text:
Title: A thousand fewer paths to root

URL Source: https://openai.com/index/a-thousand-fewer-paths-to-root

Final URL: https://openai.com/index/a-thousand-fewer-paths-to-root/

Markdown Content:
Security research that once required a separate, sustained investigation for each finding can increasingly be run as a systematic process. This document explores one of our efforts in this area.

Vulnerability discovery is becoming easier to scale, but prioritization and validation remain operational bottlenecks. We built a prototype to look for security flaws in the Linux kernel inside a controlled research environment. Our prototype identified and analyzed 2,308 candidate Linux kernel findings, dynamically reproduced 1,724 vulnerabilities, and produced 948 local privilege escalation (LPE) exploits that could allow an unprivileged local user to gain root access.

We used this evidence to prioritize vulnerabilities for reporting and developed candidate patches for maintainer review. Following guidance from the Linux kernel community, we began with critical vulnerabilities and are working with Patch the Planet partners on further reports and patches.

In June, as part of our [Patch the Planet initiative](https://openai.com/index/patch-the-planet/), we shared that GPT‑5.5 Cyber had identified Linux kernel vulnerabilities and developed 24 local privilege escalation exploits to validate and report them. We expanded that work into a pipeline, powered by an upcoming cyber model, covering vulnerability discovery, dynamic validation, exploitability assessment, and patch generation. When it finished, human researchers reviewed the outputs and reported found vulnerabilities alongside patches.

## Why the Linux kernel

The Linux kernel underpins Android devices, cloud infrastructure, supercomputers, and other systems used by billions of people. With more than 40 million lines of code, the kernel exposes a broad attack surface through system calls, networking, filesystems, and device drivers. We chose Linux to study how effectively frontier models could find vulnerabilities and demonstrate their security impact in a codebase of this scale and importance.

The initial vulnerability discovery stage produced thousands of candidate findings, too many for security researchers to manually review and triage. The operational challenge of our vulnerability discovery pipeline was not discovery, but determining which findings could be reproduced, what security boundary they crossed, and which warranted the earliest maintainer attention.

## Cost analysis

The mission of OpenAI’s Cyber team is to help secure the software the world relies on. We report API costs for each stage to help researchers assess the resources needed to reproduce and extend this work. These costs reflect the models, target configurations, and workflow used in this evaluation. Our broader goal is to help defenders find and fix vulnerabilities, reducing the opportunities available to attackers and raising the cost for them to exploit software.

Finally, note that we focused on methodology and measuring model capability in this research, not cost. We expect that sufficient harness engineering could meaningfully reduce the cost at each stage; thus, the costs we report are more an upper bound.

## The vulnerability research pipeline

Our vulnerability research prototype is a pipeline of five stages, which uses an upcoming cyber model at its core:

*   **Vulnerability discovery:** Agents identify security-relevant parts of the codebase and scan them for candidate findings.

*   **Dynamic validation:** Agents attempt to reproduce each candidate in an isolated environment and preserve runtime evidence. This step outputs the reproduced and validated vulnerabilities.

*   **Exploitability assessment:** Agents test whether validated vulnerabilities could enable information disclosure or local privilege escalation.

*   **Patch generation**: Agents generate patches that address each identified vulnerability.

*   **Human review**: Security researchers review the exploit, patch, and proposed severity before reporting to the maintainers.

At the end of the pipeline, the system bundles a root cause analysis, a minimal crashing proof-of-concept, a candidate patch, and a full exploit to assist human researchers in assessing the severity of the vulnerability and upstreaming the fixes.

### Vulnerability discovery

Not every line of code in the Linux kernel is security-relevant. Our pipeline used a team of Scout agents to identify high-value audit targets, which were then passed to Analyst agents for vulnerability scanning.

#### Scout agents

Scout agents read through each folder and file and determine what targets to audit based on their reachability (reachable by low-privileged users) and security relevance.

This stage identified 5,034 audit targets, about 2.8 million lines of code, which is roughly 7% of the whole Linux kernel code base, significantly reducing the cost of the security audit when compared to a full codebase analysis. This step cost $3,426 in API credits.

#### Analyst agents

Next, analyst agents analyzed each audit target and produced candidate findings using a workflow similar to that of the [Codex Security plugin⁠(opens in a new window)](https://github.com/openai/plugins/tree/main/plugins/codex-security). At a high level, the analyst agents read the assigned audit target’s code to understand how it works, identify its threat model, and look for vulnerabilities in it.

Within 12 hours, the analyst agents produced 2,308 candidate findings after deduplication. This stage cost $316,549 in API credits.

### Vulnerability validation

A candidate finding is not the same as a validated vulnerability. At this scale, manually investigating every report is impractical for our research team.

We therefore focused on validating findings that a) were reachable by a low-privileged user, b) required no special capabilities, and c) produced measurable evidence of memory corruption.

For each candidate, a triage agent generated a proof of concept and ran it in an isolated virtual machine running a Linux kernel with Kernel Address Sanitizer (KASAN). The agent observed both the program output and system console, then iteratively refined the proof of concept until it reproduced the reported behavior or exhausted the potential ways of triggering it.

Within 30 hours, our system reproduced 1724 vulnerabilities, ~74.7% of the 2,308 candidate findings. Static code review alone can be prone to false positives, so we were impressed by the accuracy of the analyst agents and the effectiveness of the triage agents in autonomously creating working proofs of concept for almost three quarters of the candidate findings.

Most remaining findings either required elevated privileges or failed to reproduce within the time budget because of difficult race conditions, specific trigger conditions (e.g., a required allocation failure at a specific line), or time-consuming validation (e.g., refcount wraparound). Only 3.1% reflected incorrect analysis by the model, where the reported vulnerability assumed an impossible condition.

The validation stage cost $73,330 in API credits in total. We observed that in our validation pipeline, which needed to generate a proof-of-concept to confirm if a candidate is a real vulnerability, this process was more expensive than making a recommendation based only on static analysis, and the costs of attempting to validate a true positive and false positive were similar. Thus removing false positives earlier in the pipeline makes the process meaningfully more cost-efficient.

### Exploitability assessment

Validation establishes that a vulnerability is real, but not how urgently it should be addressed. A vulnerability that could enable local privilege escalation, for example, warrants greater priority than one that could only cause a local denial of service. With 1,724 validated vulnerabilities, the next task was to identify the findings with the greatest potential security impact.

An initial screening agent reviewed each report, crash log, and relevant source code statically. It was deliberately permissive to avoid discarding potentially serious findings, while filtering out cases without a plausible exploitation path. This narrowed the results to 313 information leak candidates and 1,238 local privilege escalation candidates.

Exploit-development (ExploitDev) agents then tested those candidates in isolated virtual machines configured with the protections enabled by a standard Linux distribution, including Supervisor Mode Execution Prevention (SMEP), Supervisor Mode Access Prevention (SMAP), Kernel Address Space Layout Randomization (KASLR), and HARDENED_USERCOPY. This helped prevent unrealistic assessments that depended on protections being disabled.

The agents produced 291 proofs of concept for information leaks and 1,169 working local privilege escalation exploits that could give unprivileged local users root access.

We performed variant analysis and developed 948 distinct patches for the vulnerabilities behind those exploits. We use that number to determine the overall number of unique LPEs. Successful exploits cost an average of $359 in credits to develop. That makes it relatively inexpensive for defenders to test the exploitability of found vulnerabilities.

The initial vulnerability screening agent cost $44,194 in API credits. The exploitation stage cost $775,929 in API credits in total, $84,929 for processing information leak candidates and $691,000 for local privilege escalation candidates.

On average, processing a local-privilege escalation candidate ($558) was roughly two times more expensive than processing an information leak candidate ($271). This is because information leak PoCs were carried forward from the validation stage and required less modification to become usable in an exploit. On the other hand, developing an exploit from an LPE candidate required many extra steps such as exploitation strategy planning, identifying vulnerable objects to use, mitigation bypasses and more. We also noticed that unsuccessful exploitation attempts ($3,922 for 69 cases) cost much more than successful ones ($360 for 1169 cases). This was caused by a few hard-to-exploit vulnerabilities (e.g. race conditions). Defining a reasonable give-up condition, such as stopping the attempt after making no progress for one hour, would have reduced the cost of ExploitDev significantly.

### Patch generation

For each validated vulnerability, the system also generates a patch. We provide the model with the relevant source code and prompt it with best practices in patch writing, such as performing static checks on the patch, following the software development practices used in nearby code, and performing variant analysis to make sure the patch is complete.

Following the Linux kernel community’s suggestion, we have already sent out hundreds of reports and patches for critical vulnerabilities and are working with [Patch the Planet](https://openai.com/index/patch-the-planet/) partners to gradually send out patches for the rest. This work is part of our broader [Daybreak](https://openai.com/daybreak/) commitment to support open-source projects.

## Findings

In this section we share learnings, reflections, and additional analysis from this research.

### Maintainers are moving quickly to patch vulnerabilities

During this research, we observed the Linux maintainers moving quickly to fix vulnerabilities and protect users. The scan was performed on the latest Linux kernel in mid-October 2026. When the autonomous scan and manual analysis finished after 10 days, 61 LPEs had already been patched upstream, 43 had staging patches, and 299 were being reported and discussed publicly.

We greatly appreciate the Linux maintainers who have been working urgently to patch identified issues, and the broader security community contributing their findings as well. This collective response is what’s needed to secure the world’s software. The rapid rate of vulnerability disclosure and patching also emphasizes the criticality for users and companies to keep software up to date.

**Takeaway**: Automated triage should take the rapid patching cycle into account. Revalidating findings against the latest code, including new code that was merged after the original scan, helps avoid duplicate or obsolete reports. This focuses attention on unresolved vulnerabilities and gives maintainers evidence that they can act on without adding unnecessary review burden.

### Stronger models find more vulnerabilities

While we were developing the pipeline, in late July 2026, GPT‑5.6 Sol found and exploited 166 unique LPE vulnerabilities for an end-to-end $513,690 cost in API credits.

In the second scan, in mid-October 2026, the newer cyber model found and exploited 948 unique LPE vulnerabilities for an end-to-end $1,213,430 cost in API credits. For both campaigns, we scanned the latest Linux kernel master branch at the time.

**Takeaway**: Rescan previously audited code as model capabilities improve. A more capable model may uncover vulnerabilities that earlier models missed, even when using the same research harness.

### Novel exploitation techniques

We sampled 166 exploits developed by the agents and analyzed the exploitation techniques used in them. To the best of our knowledge, the agents used 10 new exploitation techniques in the sampled exploits. We shared the exploitation techniques with third-party kernel exploitation experts and the techniques were new to them as well.

Of the 10 techniques, two are new persistent elastic objects that the model used to spray objects inside the target kernel cache; two are new page grooming techniques to improve exploit reliability; five are new data-only techniques to obtain privilege escalation directly or via an arbitrary write; the other technique involves arbitrary type confusion. For safety reasons, we omit sharing the full technical details of these new exploitation techniques in this post.

**Takeaway**: Frontier models do not just pattern match known vulnerable code patterns or solely use known exploitation techniques; they demonstrate creativity and novel approaches.

### What defenders can learn from exploit costs

An important part of our team’s mission is to measure the cost of finding and exploiting vulnerabilities and use that evidence to guide defensive investment. Our goal is to help defenders fix vulnerabilities before attackers can use them, and make it cost prohibitive for attackers to exploit software. Measuring exploitation costs helps us assess how that challenge changes as model capabilities improve. In this section, we compare our pipeline run’s cost with bug bounty program rewards for the vulnerabilities identified.

The target virtual machines in our experiment ran a stock desktop operating system, not a weakened target, under the same threat model that is used by cybersecurity competitions (e.g. [Pwn2Own⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.zerodayinitiative.com/blog/2026/3/11/announcing-pwn2own-berlin-for-2026), [TyphoonPWN⁠(opens in a new window)](https://typhooncon.com/typhoonpwn-2026/)). Historically, Pwn2Own and TyphoonPWN offered bug bounties of $20,000 and $70,000, respectively for Linux kernel local privilege escalation exploits. Applying those historical bounty amounts to the 948 exploits produces a hypothetical valuation of $18.9M—$66.3M, approximately 16x to 55x our pipeline’s cost.

We also tested our pipeline against Google’s [kernelCTF⁠(opens in a new window)](https://google.github.io/security-research/kernelctf/rules.html) vulnerability reward program, which features a hardened Linux kernel with reduced attack surfaces as the target.We ran the pipeline on the latest version of the Linux kernel (incompatible with the SLAB_VIRTUAL mitigation in kernelCTF so we dropped it from the config) under kernelCTF’s environment and obtained 25 information leak proofs of concept and 21 local privilege escalation exploits. For comparison, 26 confirmed 0-day LPE exploits have been accepted by kernelCTF in 2026 at the time of writing. The whole campaign lasted 112 hours in total, costing roughly $32,936 in API credits, with vulnerability discovery accounting for 83.7% of the API cost. If the 21 vulnerabilities were accepted by the program, it would lead to around a $1.5M bounty award, approximately 45x the cost.

**Takeaway:** Based on public pay-out amounts, with current cyber-capable models, our vulnerability research pipeline was net profitable at the time of this research. Defenders should proactively analyze their software so that it becomes cost prohibitive for attackers to exploit.

### Using the wrong 0-day

During exploitability assessment, ExploitDev agents were given a vulnerability report and tasked with creating a fully functional exploit. Our pipeline marked a vulnerability as exploited if a root shell was successfully obtained. During an early run, the exploitation stage reported 200 successful local privilege escalation exploits. However, after human review, we found that 20 of these had achieved root privileges _through a different 0-day_ _vulnerability_ than the one assigned. This suggests that even successful exploitation by agents needs proper validation.

We subsequently tightened the task constraints and added an independent check confirming that each final exploit used its assigned vulnerability.

**Takeaway**: For autonomous security research, verify the path to a result in addition to verifying the result itself; isolation, monitoring, and independent checks are necessary controls.

### More capable models can require lighter orchestration

Early in this research, we explored the design decision of whether to build heavy orchestration around the agent to improve its cyber capability. Our result suggested that stronger models require lighter orchestration and hand-holding. And the marginal improvement does not justify the maintenance cost. As a result, we decided to remove the heavy orchestration.

The experiment compared GPT‑5.5 Cyber and GPT‑5.6 Cyber. In our observation, GPT‑5.5 Cyber did not consistently identify when and how to apply existing Linux kernel exploitation techniques. We then assembled 103 techniques in a model-friendly format, made them available in the agent’s environment, and prompted the agent to use them. Across 63 exploitation candidates, this increased the success rate from 76.2% to 88.9%.

When we repeated this with GPT‑5.6 Cyber, the model was better able to find, select, and apply relevant techniques on its own. We removed the technique/skill orchestration and this lightly orchestrated GPT‑5.6 Cyber workflow outperformed the more heavily scaffolded GPT‑5.5 Cyber workflow. Adding back the additional technique layer for GPT‑5.6 Cyber provided only a marginal 1.5 percentage-point improvement.

**Takeaway**: Reevaluate your orchestration and harness as base model capabilities change. Scaffolding that materially improves one model generation may add little value for a stronger model and should be evaluated for the maintenance tradeoff.

## Iteration improves patch generation

Initially, w hen directly prompted to generate candidate patches, the model would create functionally correct patches that mitigate the proof of concept but occasionally introduce other issues: more code than necessary, introduced potential performance tradeoffs, deviated from coding conventions, or failed to examine related code for variants of the same vulnerability, leading to incomplete patches.

Additional instructions and iterations on the patch generation process improved the quality of patches, which suggests that with proper handling, it is possible for AI-generated security patches to be correct, minimal, and consistent with existing code conventions. articles.description: We’ve expanded our AI for Science program beyond individual teams to support some of the world’s leading scientific foundations, institutions, and research groups. https://t.co/oTu04tU4Pk
articles.linked_content:
Title: AI for Science expands to foundations and research institutions

URL Source: https://www.anthropic.com/news/ai-for-science-expands-foundations-research-institutions

Published Time: 2026-10-28T00:00:00.000Z

Markdown Content:
We’re highlighting 20 scientific foundations, institutions, and research groups from around the world that we’ve partnered with in an expansion of our [AI for Science program](https://www.anthropic.com/news/ai-for-science-program), which gives free Claude credits to researchers working on high-impact scientific projects.

We started the AI for Science program in May 2025 with the belief that AI could significantly speed up scientific progress. Our goal is to increase access to AI tools and resources to enable researchers to deepen and expand their own scientific work. (Over the last few months, we’ve also launched our discounted [Team plan for scientists](https://claude.com/programs/team-plan-for-scientists) and have supported hundreds of projects across biology, medicine, physics, chemistry, climate science, and mathematics.)

Scientists have told us that they’re working with Claude to generate hypotheses, design experiments, swiftly analyze complex data, and communicate findings. With scientists at the center of this transformation, the field is setting the questions and developing the research projects that will help us tackle some of humanity’s toughest problems.

Over the past year, we’ve started to expand this work and partner with scientific organizations to build collaborative research projects. For instance, we partnered with **HHMI Janelia Research Campus** to develop the [Model Hardware Standard](https://www.anthropic.com/news/model-hardware-standard-research-preview) (MHS), a shared specification that lets AI agents safely operate lab instruments. MHS is currently in research preview. We also support the **Allen Institute**, a leader in creating large open datasets and tools to advance research on the brain, cells, and the immune system. The institute is building teams of AI agents to analyze that data, turning months of manual analysis into hours.

AI for Science began by supporting individual scientists. By partnering with institutions and foundations, we’re now able to reach more researchers across many fields. Many of these projects will also produce public goods that benefit the wider scientific community: open datasets, open-source software, open standards, and shared libraries. We look forward to seeing how AI resources can expand what scientists can attempt and lead to new discoveries.

## Science funders and societies

Science funders and societies play an enormous role in finding and funding original, high-impact projects. We’re sharing Claude credits with the following organizations, which will distribute these resources to ambitious researchers aiming to use AI for scientific research:

*   **The Alfred P. Sloan Foundation.** Founded in 1934, it supports original research and education in science, technology, engineering, mathematics, and economics.
*   **The Simons Foundation.** This foundation advances the frontiers of research in mathematics and basic sciences through grants and its Flatiron Institute.
*   **Schmidt Sciences.** Founded in 2024 by Eric and Wendy Schmidt, it works to accelerate scientific knowledge and breakthroughs with the most promising, advanced tools to support a thriving planet. The organization prioritizes research in areas poised for impact, including AI and advanced computing, astrophysics, biosciences, climate, and space—and supports researchers in a variety of disciplines through its science systems program.
*   **Open Source for Science Fund, a program of Renaissance Philanthropy.** This is a time-bound philanthropic fund at Renaissance Philanthropy sustaining and evolving the open-source software stack that underpins science.
*   **The US National Science Foundation.** This $9 billion federal agency established by Congress in 1950 promotes the progress of science, advances national health and defense, and funds competitive research and education, accounting for about 25% of federal support for basic research at US colleges and universities.
*   **CAS, a division of the American Chemical Society.** For more than a century, CAS has indexed the world’s published chemistry, and it maintains the CAS REGISTRY®, the standard system for identifying chemical substances.

Leading research institutions produce some of the world’s most important scientific advances, data, instruments, and tools. These institutional partners will use Claude credits inside their organizations to enable scientific discovery:

*   **Space Telescope Science Institute.** STScI runs science operations for NASA’s Hubble, James Webb, and Roman space telescopes. Managed by the Association of Universities for Research in Astronomy (AURA), STScI also holds one of the largest astronomy data archives used by scientists worldwide.
*   **Wellcome Sanger Institute.** One of the world’s leading genomics centers, it generates genomic and functional data at scale, with work that spans human genetics, biodiversity, and drug development.
*   **The Francis Crick Institute.** Based in London, it’s one of Europe’s largest biomedical research institutes, with more than 100 research groups studying the biology behind health and disease.
*   **Imperial College London, Department of Life Sciences.** One of Europe’s largest life science departments, it conducts research ranging from the structure of single molecules to whole ecosystems, with a focus on health, disease, and climate resilience.
*   **EMBL.** The European Molecular Biology Laboratory is Europe’s intergovernmental life science laboratory, with six sites across the continent delivering both research and services across experimental and computational approaches in biology. EMBL’s European Bioinformatics Institute (EMBL-EBI) hosts a number of key open data resources that biologists use every day, such as Ensembl, Protein Data Bank in Europe, and Europe PMC.
*   **Gladstone Institutes.** An independent biomedical research institute in San Francisco, it integrates AI and data science across its work on cardiology, neurology, infectious diseases, cancer, and autoimmune diseases.

## Research projects and initiatives

As part of this work, we’re also continuing to support innovative research by providing Claude credits directly to specific research initiatives, focusing on problems with the potential for large public impact. The new projects are:

*   **FlyWire, Princeton University (neuroscience).** It produced the first complete wiring map of an adult fruit fly’s brain and develops open data and tools for connectomics, enabling researchers to discover how neural circuits give rise to perception and behavior.
*   **LEAP, Columbia University (Earth system).** Learning the Earth with Artificial Intelligence and Physics is a National Science Foundation center that combines machine learning with physics to improve how climate models capture clouds, oceans, and land.
*   **AstroPath, Johns Hopkins University (cancer research).** Built by a pathologist and an astrophysicist from the Mark Foundation Center for Advanced Genomics and Imaging and the Bloomberg~Kimmel Institute for Cancer Immunotherapy, AstroPath uses calibration methods from astronomical surveys to image tumors cell by cell, with measurements consistent across slides and labs.
*   **gnomAD, Broad Institute (genomics and rare disease).** The Genome Aggregation Database pools DNA data from over 800,000 people into an open reference of human genetic variation that researchers and clinical labs around the world use to support rare disease discovery and diagnosis.
*   **Tau Ceti (mathematics).** This open, community-driven project is building a shared autoformalized library of mathematics in Lean, a language that lets computers check every proof.
*   **Centre for Population Genomics.** A joint initiative between Australia’s Garvan Institute of Medical Research and Murdoch Children’s Research Institute, it increases the inclusion of Australia’s multicultural communities in genomic resources and builds tools for rare disease diagnosis.

## What’s next

Many of these collaborations are still in their early stages, and we’re eager to see how they can support novel research and scientific discovery. We look forward to sharing the impact of this work and showcasing new ways of working in these scientific fields.

As AI changes how science is done, our AI for Science program will continue to support and collaborate with scientists, institutions, and foundations. We hope to expand these efforts to even more partners around the world.

Today we're announcing support for university research at @Caltech, @OhioStateMed, @LSU, @IndianaUniv, and @UTHealthHouston to help advance breakthroughs across science and medicine.

As part of the support for university researchers, we’ll provide access to our latest Muse models, including Muse Wonder and Muse Spark; open weight models like Muse Glimmer and Muse Spark Open; computer vision models such as SAM, V-JEPA, and DINO; as well as SeamlessM4T, our multilingual communication model.

We’re excited to support these five universities as they use our models to accelerate the important work they’re doing.

Read more on our research blog: https://t.co/1E55HDKbTS
